name: The Kingdom of Benin
title: Social Hierarchy of the Kingdom of Benin: From Oba to Enslaved
period: c. 1440–1690 (from Oba Ewuare to the civil war of the 1690s)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are held to be sacred and leave the palace only for great ceremonies; every chief of the palace and the town owes his title to you, and the kingdom’s brass, ivory and coral are yours.
tiers.kid: The Oba was Benin’s king, and his people believed he was sacred.
tiers.rise: The throne passed within the royal line, in principle to the eldest son, but brothers fought for it: after Ozolua’s death Esigie overthrew his brother Arhuaran. In the 17th century reigns grew short, the father-to-son line may have broken after Ohuan’s death in 1641, and the chiefs’ power grew.
tiers.why: The Oba was a sacred king.

tiers.name: Hereditary chiefs
tiers.you: Your title came to you from your father; you will help crown the next Oba, but since Ewuare’s reforms you no longer choose him.
tiers.kid: The Uzama were chiefs who inherited their titles and crowned each new Oba.
tiers.rise: Birth alone made an Uzama: the titles were inherited. What the Uzama could lose was power, as Ewuare’s reforms showed.
tiers.why: The Uzama were the senior hereditary chiefs of Benin, and their titles passed from father to son.

tiers.name: Palace chiefs
tiers.you: You hold a title the Oba gave you after long service in a palace association; you help keep his regalia and wardrobe, attend his person or run the quarters of his wives.
tiers.kid: Palace chiefs looked after the Oba’s treasures and household, and the Oba chose them himself.
tiers.rise: Service in a palace association was the usual road to a palace title, which only the Oba could confer and which did not pass to the holder’s sons.
tiers.why: Oba Ewuare is credited with creating the palace chiefs, the Eghaevbo n’Ogbe, as one of two orders of chiefs appointed by the Oba and answerable to him.

tiers.name: Town chiefs
tiers.you: The Oba gave you your title, not your father; you collect tribute, hear disputes and may lead men to war under the Iyase.
tiers.kid: Town chiefs collected tribute for the Oba, and their leader, the Iyase, led armies in war.
tiers.rise: The Oba conferred town titles, often on men who had proved themselves in war; a son did not inherit his father’s title.
tiers.why: The town chiefs, the Eghaevbo n’Ore, formed the second order of appointed chiefs that Ewuare is credited with creating.

tiers.name: Royal craft guilds
tiers.term: Igun Eronmwon (brass casters), Igun Ematon (blacksmiths), Igbesanmwan (ivory and wood carvers)
tiers.you: You were born into the casters’ ward and cast brass for the Oba, who alone may own what you make.
tiers.kid: Benin’s brass casters made famous metal heads and plaques for the Oba’s palace.
tiers.rise: Most members were born into their guild’s ward. A guild’s fortunes rose and fell with the power of the Oba it served.
tiers.why: Ewuare is credited with dividing Benin City into separate quarters for different crafts, and its craftsmen were organised in guilds that worked for the court.

tiers.name: Free villagers
tiers.you: You farm yams in a village run by its elders, send tribute to the capital through the chiefs and are called up with the village regiments when the Oba goes to war.
tiers.kid: Most people in Benin were farmers who lived in villages led by their elders.
tiers.rise: A freeborn man could move to the capital and enter a palace association, the first step towards a title, and war brought rewards. A crime could lead to execution or sale into slavery.
tiers.why: Most of the Oba’s subjects were free farmers in the villages outside the capital, Edo-speaking in the heartland and of many other peoples in the conquered lands.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You are one of the captives of the wars, part of a chief’s labour force and one of his fighting men; he may sell you, even to European traders.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; many were captives from wars.
tiers.rise: People became slaves through capture in war, a criminal conviction or tribute from subject towns; the sources for this period say little about how any left slavery.
tiers.why: Slavery was part of Benin’s order.
